questions.q: What is the test for whether a project's dashboard is finished, according to the one-page result idea?
options: You can state each side of the result in one sentence with a verdict
It has at least 20 components
It uses every report type
It has been shared with everyone
questions.explain: If you cannot summarize each side in a sentence, the dashboard still lacks a clear message.

questions.q: Which item belongs on the pre-presentation checklist?
options: Adding more decorative colors
Removing all definitions to save space
Testing every filter on every component and documenting the cleaning steps
Waiting for the next data refresh to guess the numbers
questions.explain: Definitions, filter behavior, running user, refresh and cleaning documentation are what make the numbers trustworthy.

questions.q: What are the five sections of the portfolio write-up?
options: Title, abstract, index, glossary, appendix
Problem, approach, design decisions, results, limits and next steps
Data, chart, legend, axis, title
Login, dashboard, report, filter, logout
questions.explain: The write-up mirrors the presentation: the problem, the approach, the design decisions, the results, then limits and next steps.

questions.q: Which data is safe to use in a public portfolio piece?
options: A real employer's customer list with names blurred halfway
Confidential figures if you add a disclaimer
Any data you can export
Data from a Developer Edition org or sample data
questions.explain: Use Developer Edition or sample data. Never include confidential employer or customer data in a portfolio.

questions.q: How should you treat limits you found, such as hand-maintained quota or missing history?
options: Present them as evidence for next steps, such as snapshots or CRM Analytics and Tableau
Hide them
Treat them as proof you failed
Remove the affected KPIs silently
questions.explain: Honest limits build trust and point to the next improvement. Hiding them undermines credibility.
